notes.b: Individuals address barriers by acting for themselves and for others.
points: Self-advocacy: a person states their own needs and asks clubs, schools or coaches to change how activities are run.
Forming or joining groups: people who share a barrier set up their own club or walking group, run by its members.
Becoming coaches, leaders or role models: people who have overcome a barrier show others that it can be done.
Campaigning: individuals lobby local clubs and local authorities for accessible facilities, subsidised places or inclusive timetables.
Social media: individuals post videos and updates to raise awareness of their group's needs and to recruit others to join.
Choosing or adapting activities: a person selects an activity that suits their ability and adjusts its rules or equipment to take part.

notes.b: Representative groups speak for a group's interests and run or lobby for opportunities for it.
points: Disability sport organisations: Paralympics Ireland governs Paralympic sport in Ireland and lobbies for opportunities for disabled athletes.
Cara is a national organisation supporting the inclusion of people with disabilities in sport.
Sport Against Racism Ireland (SARI) runs anti-racism and inclusion programmes through sport and campaigns against racism.
Special Olympics Ireland provides sport for people with intellectual disability and represents its athletes.
Women-in-sport bodies and older people's organisations represent their members' interests with clubs and sports bodies.
Programmes and training: representative groups run programmes and training for members and give advice to clubs on including them.
Awareness campaigns and lobbying: representative groups campaign to change attitudes and lobby decision-makers for funding and better provision.

notes.b: Voluntary organisations are run by volunteers or charities rather than by the state.
points: Special Olympics clubs give people with intellectual disability regular sport in a club setting, run largely by volunteers.
Local walking groups give older adults a regular, low-cost way to be active.
Community sports clubs use volunteer coaches and committees to offer local sessions open to all members of the community.

notes.b: Statutory organisations are set up by law and funded by the state.
points: Sport Ireland provides funding, policy and programmes for sport and physical activity nationally.
Local Sports Partnerships are state-funded networks that deliver sport and physical activity programmes in local areas.
Sports Inclusion Disability Officers work within Local Sports Partnerships to help clubs and schools include people with disabilities.
Local authorities provide public facilities such as parks and sports grounds, and fund local programmes.
The Department of Education sets policy for school physical education and sport.
Cost: subsidised or free programmes and an equipment loan scheme.
Facilities: accessible design of venues, with grants to pay for upgrades.
Lack of trained coaches: inclusion training for coaches and leaders.
Lack of confidence: beginner sessions, single-sex sessions and buddy systems.
Transport: local provision close to home and school-based provision.
Negative attitudes: awareness campaigns and role models.
Poor media coverage: campaigns that press for more coverage of under-represented sport.
Barrier: few visible female role models, so girls rarely see women succeeding in sport.
Who: the 20x20 campaign, launched in 2018 to increase the visibility of women's sport in Ireland.
How: the campaign's slogan, 'If she can't see it, she can't be it', put visibility of women's sport at the centre of its message.
Effect: the campaign aimed to give girls and women role models they can see, which is the barrier it targeted.
Second barrier: few female coaches. Who: individual women who train as coaches and leaders. How: they lead sessions as visible role models. Effect: girls have a role model in the coaching role.
Barrier: lack of trained coaches and inaccessible facilities.
Who: Sports Inclusion Disability Officers within Local Sports Partnerships, a statutory response.
How: the officers work with clubs and schools to make their activities inclusive and to connect disabled people with suitable sessions.
Effect: clubs and schools have a named source of advice on including disabled people.

Second barrier: lack of adapted equipment. Who: an individual disabled athlete or parent. How: self-advocacy, asking a club or school to provide or lend adapted equipment. Effect: the request puts the need on the club's agenda.
Barrier: fear of injury or falling, and lack of confidence.
Who: Go for Life, run by Age & Opportunity with Sport Ireland support, a national programme for older people.
How: structured activity designed for older adults' ability and needs, delivered in local groups.
Effect: older adults have a supported route into activity, which aims to build their confidence over time.
What has worked: campaigns and programmes with one clear target group, which give visible role models and structured access.
Gap: rural provision is thin, so people far from towns and clubs have fewer options.
Gap: funding is often short-term, so successful programmes can end when money runs out.
Gap: reliance on volunteers, so coaching and leadership are stretched and hard to sustain.
Test: a response works when the barrier is removed for the people it targets, which shows in who takes part rather than in the number of programmes offered.

keyTerms.definition: A person speaking up for their own needs and asking for changes to how activity is provided.
An organisation that speaks for a group's interests and runs or lobbies for opportunities for that group.
A body run by volunteers or charities, such as a community sports club.
A body set up by law and funded by the state, such as Sport Ireland.
Persuading decision-makers to change policy or to provide opportunities.
Pairing a participant with a partner who helps them take part in a session.
A state-funded network that delivers sport and physical activity programmes in local areas.
A campaign that aims to change attitudes and raise the visibility of a group.

factCards.definition: Sport Ireland, Local Sports Partnerships, local authorities and the Department of Education.
Special Olympics clubs, local walking groups and community sports clubs.
Launched in 2018 to increase the visibility of women's sport in Ireland, with the slogan 'If she can't see it, she can't be it'.
Rural provision, short-term funding and reliance on volunteers.

questions.prompt: Discuss ways in which barriers to participation for one group have been addressed by representative groups and by statutory organisations.
questions.model: The group is people with physical disability, whose barriers include inaccessible facilities and transport, lack of adapted equipment, untrained coaches, cost and negative attitudes. Representative groups address these first. Paralympics Ireland governs Paralympic sport in Ireland and lobbies for opportunities for disabled athletes, so it champions adapted competition and visible pathways. Cara, a national organisation supporting inclusion of people with disabilities in sport, works to remove the barriers that keep disabled people out of sport. Representative groups also run awareness campaigns that challenge negative attitudes. Statutory organisations provide funding, policy and facilities. Sport Ireland and Local Sports Partnerships fund and deliver programmes, and Sports Inclusion Disability Officers within Local Sports Partnerships advise clubs and schools on including disabled people, which addresses untrained coaches and clubs that have not adapted their activities. Local authorities provide facilities that can be made accessible. Representative groups push for change and build awareness, while statutory bodies supply the money, policy and local staff to act on it. Their effect depends on funding and on whether local clubs act on the advice.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways a barrier to participation for people with a disability could be overcome.
questions.model: Barrier: inaccessible facilities. First way: accessible design of venues, such as step-free access and accessible changing rooms, with grants to pay for the upgrades. Second way: a barrier of untrained coaches could be overcome by inclusion training for coaches, delivered with help from a Sports Inclusion Disability Officer in a Local Sports Partnership, so that coaches can adapt sessions for disabled participants.
